[2:38] the expertise in mercantile activity and sailing the Genoese possessed was far too valuable.

[4:13] If such a venture to the west failed, only relatively minor funds would be wasted, but

[4:24] taking? On September 6th, 1492, Columbus set off on his journey from the Canary Islands

[7:52] August 11th, 1492, Borgia took the papal throne. Upon receiving the envoys from Ferdinand and
[8:00] Isabella, whom Borgia had always viewed favourably, in April 1493, the Pope began taking into
[8:06] account the precedents set in rulings from previous decades, and issued the first of
[8:11] three edicts. Its name was inter caetera. This edict was known as a ‘papal bull’,
[8:18] named after the bulla seal used to authenticate a public decree made by the pope, and was

[8:30] claim on the new world discovered by the Spanish and Portuguese crowns, and provided a justification
[8:36] for the conquest of the Americas for centuries to come. Moreover, they were the wedge that
[8:43] drove European nations into centuries of intermittent warfare over colonial wealth and prestige.
[8:48] The first inter caetera, dated May 3rd, 1493, granted Spain the exclusive right to travel
[8:57] in, trade with or colonise the discovered lands, provided they were not already the
[9:02] possession of a Christian ruler. However, the wording of this bull was quite vague,
[9:08] much to the dissatisfaction of the Catholic Majesties. So, they again sent ambassadors
[9:13] to the pope. Instead of begging the Pope for a favour, the Spanish ambassadors chastised
[9:19] Borgia’s lack of support for his native land, as he was by birth a native of Aragon.
[9:25] It was suggested that Ferdinand might hesitate in the future to offer military aid to the
[9:30] papacy. This was crucial, as the French king Charles VIII claimed sovereignty over Naples,
[9:37] and would have to march through Rome to get there. These political pressures led to two
[9:42] new papal bulls, which were more favorable to the Catholic Monarchs.
[9:47] The second edict, known as Eximiae Devotionis, clarified and rephrased the first bull. It
[9:54] placed emphasis on the rights granted to Portugal in ‘Africa, Guinea, and the Gold Mine, and
[9:59] elsewhere’ in previous decades, whilst granting Spain those same rights over the lands to
[10:04] the west which had been discovered by Columbus. Concluding the trio was the second inter caetera.
[10:12] The vague language of the first was replaced by a precise line of demarcation in the middle
[10:17] of the Atlantic Ocean, drawn arbitrarily on a north-south boundary around 100 leagues
[10:23] west of the Azores and Cape Verde. All lands to the east of the demarcation line would
[10:28] belong to Portugal, while all lands to the west would be under Spanish dominion. No other
[10:34] ships were legally allowed to sail in these waters without the consent of these empires.
[10:40] As the word of the bulls spread, the resounding implications of Borgia’s act became clearer
[10:45] to all. Columbus was quickly arranging his second voyage, while Joao II was furious at
[10:52] being diplomatically outmaneuvered. However, just as Spain’s monopoly over the vast regions
[10:57] west of the demarcation line had been secured by papal decree, so too had the pope secured

[11:10] to the west, fearing it would undermine his own gains.
[11:13] The pope was probably was rushed by the necessity of averting a potentially devastating war
[11:19] between Christendom’s most powerful nations. Nevertheless, Joao II immediately objected,
[11:25] not satisfied with any decision that might hinder Portuguese maritime opportunities at
[11:30] the very moment his naval strength was at its height. Still, Joao did not dare to launch

[11:54] In the March of 1494, a delegation of Portuguese officials visited Spain and, after months
[12:00] of debate, eventually reached a historic agreement on June 7th - the Treaty of Tordesillas. It
[12:07] was mostly just a reaffirmation of the papal bulls’ conditions, but had a few additions.

[15:44] through Portugal’s ‘half’ of the world to get home, and they had also taken spices
